The first advanced composite material used in aircraft was Gordon Aerolite in 1940.
Aerolite had an ultimate tensile stress of 70,000 psi and a Young's modulus of 7.0 x 10^6 psi.
Redux bonding was developed during WWII to improve metal-to-metal joints over rivets.
Boron fibers have a density of 2.6 g/cm³ and diameter around 100 μm.
Carbon fibers have densities around 1.8–1.85 g/cm³ and diameters about 8 μm.
Arall is a hybrid composite of aluminum alloy and aramid epoxy pre-preg.
Glare composite uses glass fiber and toughened epoxy for better compressive strength.
Grumman's F14A Tomcat used boron/epoxy composites for the horizontal stabilizer, saving 82 kg.
The Airbus A320 uses composites for 15% of its airframe weight, including two tonnes of carbon fiber.
Composite vertical fin on the Airbus A340 is 20% lighter than the aluminum equivalent and has fewer parts.
Composite manufacturing techniques include profiling pre-preg, hand lay-up, tape laying, filament winding, tape winding, resin injection molding, and braiding.
Tooling materials for composites include metal, graphite, ceramic, and nickel electroforming.
Adhesive bonding is preferred for composite joints but mechanical fasteners are used where necessary.
Computer-aided design and finite element analysis are critical for accurate composite structure design.
Thermosetting resins are most widely used; thermoplastics like PEEK are emerging for some applications.
Fiber orientation is typically at 0°, 45°, or 90° to tailor anisotropic strength properties.
Pre-preg materials allow controlled resin content and fiber alignment for better quality.
Composite radomes are produced by resin injection molding with syntactic foam cores.
Composite structures offer high specific strength and stiffness, corrosion resistance, and fatigue performance.
Weight savings from composites reduce fuel consumption and operating costs significantly.
